description:
My strengths are research, planning, idea design, system architecture, problem-solving and meticulous attention to detail. I can shape the concept, design the gameplay and mission logic, plan execution and collaborate closely with developers to bring our ideas to life.

Who I’m looking for: Game developers, game designers and UI/UX designers are especially welcome. Anyone with a solid plan, creative ideas or relevant skills wish to make the team great is encouraged to join.
summary: Moon Farm is a free farm-style game for kids aged 7 to 12. Kids run a Moon or Mars outpost for four astronauts they name themselves. Power, air, food and radiation compete: the shield uses power, greenhouses need power to grow food, Moon nights remove the sun, and help from Earth arrives days late. Surprise events give 10 seconds to choose, and every option costs something. The solar flares kids face are real flares from NASA's DONKI database, shown with their real class and date, so a shielding decision is linked to actual space weather. It answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real deep-space trade-offs into play, so children feel why astronauts must budget every watt, breath and meal. It runs in any browser and as an Android app, with no account needed.
details:
What it does and how it works: Kids manage an outpost across five themed pages (Power, Air, Food, Radiation, Crew). Solar panels make power; machines (oxygen maker, greenhouses, shield, lab) use it; a battery stores extra, and a brownout stops machines. Every 5th Moon day is night with no sun, and dust slowly lowers panel power until the player cleans it. The crew uses air and food every day. Greenhouses need power and two days to grow, and the player picks the plants. Radiation only goes up; the shield cuts it by 25% per level but costs power. Calling Earth brings supplies after 2 days (Moon) or 4 days (Mars) to teach communication delay. Random events (dust storm, solar flare, meteorite, supply capsule, helper rover) give 10 seconds to choose, and every option costs something. The flare events use real flares from NASA DONKI: X-class needs a level 3 shield, M-class level 2, C-class level 1. Offline, the game reuses saved NASA data and says so.

Benefits and intended impact: A child finishes a game understanding that astronauts budget power, air, food and radiation, and that space weather is real. Each page has a mini-game, an About page (what it is, how it works in the game, how it works in real space) and a Watch section with five short animated videos of what happens in a solar storm or when power, food or air runs out. Explorer mode shows the formulas for older siblings and classrooms. New systems unlock slowly (radiation on day 3, dust on day 4) so young players are not overwhelmed.

Creativity: real flares become gameplay; a different themed page for each resource; astronauts the child names; Quran and space reflection cards; an original organ-style soundtrack generated by code.

Factors we considered: plain words for ages 7 to 12, no free safe choices, a gentle start, replayability, and honesty about data. The screen says what is live, saved or archived. Game numbers such as the Moon radiation rate are simplified for play and are labeled as such.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework; Web Audio; NASA DONKI API; Capacitor for Android; GitHub Pages; a Node.js and jsdom playtest bot (480 automated play-throughs per version for balance).

AI disclosure: The code, the music-generating code, the in-game text and the documents were written with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic). The team directed the concept, then reviewed and tested the work. No AI-generated images or video are used, and no NASA logos appear.
